QDISC-1325               Joseph's monotheistic preaching and Muhammad's mission            Strong are structurally linked

records.title: 12:110 interpretive difficulty
bodyParagraphs: QDISC-1326 — 12:110 interpretive difficulty Do not flatten this verse into one uncontroversial English rendering.
It belongs in our cumulative study of:
prophetic certainty, divine promises, variant readings, and later theological pressure on translation.
Status: OPEN / Arabic-reading investigation warranted if needed.
No QI yet because the underlying Arabic and referents must first be established.
12:111 — The key closing claim The final verse says:
“In their stories there is certainly a lesson for people of understanding.”
“but a confirmation of what is before it…”
plus guidance and mercy for believers. The wording is preserved in early Qur'anic manuscript witnesses catalogued by Corpus Coranicum.                   Corpus Coranicu… +1
This is extremely important for our entire project.
QDISC-1326               12:110 has significant reading/referent difficulty                OPEN

QDISC-1326 — Q12:110 textual/qirāʾāt investigation This verse genuinely deserves the flag. The ambiguity is ancient, and early Muslims themselves recognized that one interpretation creates a serious theological problem about prophetic confidence in God's promises.
‫َح َّت ٰى ِإَذا اْس َت ْيَأَس الُّرُس ُل َو َظ ُّن وا َأَّن ُه ْم َق ْد ُكِذ ُب وا َج اَءُه ْم َن ْصُر َن ا‬
The unvocalized consonantal skeleton permits readings whose difference cannot be seen from the bare rasm alone.

The reading tradition preserves two major passive forms. The qirāʾāt sources record the light reading among figures including Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās and others, while the strengthened reading became the reading of most of the Seven.                Tafsir +1
kudhibū                                                           ‫“ُكِذ ُبوا‬they were lied to / had been given something false”
There is also reported active/light interpretation associated with early authorities in which the people think the messengers have spoken falsely.                       Tafsir
So this isn't merely modern translators disagreeing. The difficulty is embedded in the early reading and exegetical traditions.
2. Reading A — kudhdhibū: “the messengers were rejected as liars” This is the much easier theological reading:
“Until, when the messengers despaired and became convinced that they had been rejected as liars, Our help came to them.”
→ messengers despair of their people's belief
→ they realize their communities have rejected them
This produces no doubt about God whatsoever.
A modern translation such as Sahih International essentially follows this direction:
the messengers despaired and were certain “that they had been denied.”                                 Quran +1
3. Reading B — kudhibū: the difficult reading The lighter form potentially produces:
the messengers despaired and thought that they had been lied to.
If the subject of ẓannū remains al-rusul — the messengers, the surface reading can sound like:
the messengers thought the promised divine assistance might not actually come.
That interpretation is attested in early exegetical transmission.
Al-Ṭabarī preserves a report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās explaining that the messengers were human beings who became weak/despaired.                   King Saud Unive…
And this is exactly what provoked a famous response attributed to ʿĀʾisha.
4. ʿĀʾisha strongly rejects that interpretation The early report preserved through ʿUrwa has ʿĀʾisha asked about this verse.
When confronted with the possibility that the messengers thought God's promise to them might have failed, she responds:
God never told His messenger something without the messenger knowing that it would occur.

She instead understood the verse so that the prophets came to think their followers had rejected them, after the ordeal became prolonged. Al-Ṭabarī preserves the dispute, and later exegetes also transmit it.
It shows that early Muslims themselves recognized:
One possible reading/interpretation appears to imply prophetic doubt concerning a divine promise.
And ʿĀʾisha rejected that implication on theological grounds.
5. But Ibn ʿAbbās traditions are themselves divided This gets even more interesting.
Reports attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās are not uniform.
One tradition gives the difficult interpretation:
But other material attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās interprets the pronouns differently:
messengers despair of their people's belief
the people think the messengers have lied to them.
Likewise, reports associated with Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Mujāhid preserve this solution.    King Saud Unive… +1
So the light reading itself does not require prophets doubting God.
6. This produces three historically attested interpretive models
Messengers despair of converting their people
→ know that their people have rejected them as liars
Model B — People think prophets lied kudhibū
→ people think the messengers' promised judgment/help was false
Model C — Messengers experience doubt under extreme distress kudhibū
→ think the promised assistance has somehow failed / that they have been given a false expectation
This is the difficult reading rejected by ʿĀʾisha but preserved in early exegetical transmission attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās and others.             Quran Tafsir +1
7. Therefore the Arabic itself does not force prophetic doubt This is the critical conclusion.
It would be incorrect to say:
“Q12:110 says prophets thought God lied to them.”
The textual tradition doesn't permit that level of certainty.
But it would also be incorrect to say:
“There has never been any such interpretation.”
The fact that ʿĀʾisha reportedly responds “God forbid!” shows how seriously the alternative was taken.
8. There is an additional issue: ẓannū — “they thought” Even under the safer kudhdhibū reading, commentators noticed something:
If the messengers already knew their people had rejected them, why say:
ʿĀʾisha's reported interlocutor raises essentially this objection: if they knew their people had called them liars, why call it ẓann?
Her response maintains that the relevant uncertainty concerned the followers' perseverance, not God's truthfulness.         King Saud Unive…
This demonstrates that the problem isn't only one missing shadda.
‫َح َّت ٰى ِإَذا اْس َت ْيَأَس الُّرُس ُل َو َظ ُّن وا َأَّن ُه ْم َق ْد ُكِذ ُب وا َج اَءُه ْم َن ْصُر َن ا‬
“they had been lied to / something promised appeared false.”
Also early and well attested in the reading/exegetical tradition.                          Tafsir +1
Interpretations A. Messengers thought their people had rejected them. No theological difficulty.
B. People thought the messengers had lied. No prophetic doubt.
C. Messengers themselves temporarily feared that what they had been promised would not occur. Early interpretation attested; theologically difficult.
Early Islamic dispute ʿĀʾisha explicitly rejects Model C with “God forbid,” arguing that prophets did not doubt what God had told them.         King Saud Unive… +1

Reports attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās preserve more than one interpretive trajectory, so we should not manufacture a simple “Ibn ʿAbbās versus ʿĀʾisha” binary.                           King Saud Unive… +1
Confidence Existence of reading variation: VERY HIGH.
Existence of early interpretive dispute: VERY HIGH.
ʿĀʾisha's rejection of prophet-doubts-God interpretation: strongly transmitted.
Arabic requiring prophets to doubt God: NO.
Arabic completely excluding that ancient interpretation: NO.
QI status I would not create a QI contradiction here.
The Qur'an elsewhere presents God's promises as reliable, but 12:110 has enough genuine reading/pronominal ambiguity that we cannot establish:
Qur'an proposition A: God never fails His promise
Qur'an proposition B: prophets knew God had lied.
The latter proposition is simply not textually secure.

QDISC-1327 — Surah 12 calls itself confirmation, despite substantial narrative differences The Qur'an has just retold Joseph while differing from Genesis in numerous details:
Genesis has Joseph tell the brothers his dreams; Qur'an has Jacob tell him not to.
Genesis has Jacob deceived by the bloody garment; Qur'anic Jacob rejects the story.
Genesis has brothers sell Joseph; Qur'anic caravan apparently sells him.
Genesis lacks the women cutting their hands.
Genesis lacks the front/back shirt test.
Genesis lacks Joseph's prison anti-idolatry sermon.
Genesis has Potiphar's wife maintain her accusation; Qur'an has her confess.
Genesis has Joseph leave prison immediately; Qur'an has him demand vindication.
Genesis keeps Joseph's identity hidden from Benjamin; Qur'an has private disclosure.
Genesis has cup-divination; Qur'an omits it.
Genesis has Jacob believe Joseph dead; Qur'an has him search for Joseph.
Genesis lacks white eyes, Joseph's scent and sight-restoring shirt.
Therefore taṣdīq cannot automatically mean verbatim narrative identity.
That is a major hermeneutical finding.
QDISC-1327               Qur'an calls itself confirmation despite substantial Joseph       Major scripture-relation finding narrative differences

records.title: “Confirmation” ≠ “identical reproduction”
bodyParagraphs: Therefore when later evaluating Qur'anic statements that it “confirms” Torah/Gospel, we cannot simply assume the Qur'an means:
every narrative detail must be identical.
The Qur'an apparently understands confirmation at a broader level—truth, prophetic message, divine origin, theological continuity, correction/clarification, or some combination thereof.
Which of those meanings dominates must be determined contextually.
This should become a major cross-reference for our continuing Tawrāt/Injīl/taḥrīf investigation.
QDISC-1328               Qur'anic taṣdīq cannot simply mean identical narrative            Major hermeneutical finding reproduction

bodyParagraphs: Original heading/title: — “Detailed explanation of everything” must be
QDISC-1329 — “Detailed explanation of everything” must be contextualized ‫َو َت ْفِص يَل ُك ِّل َشْي ٍء‬
It obviously cannot mean the Qur'an contains every possible fact about reality—Surah 12 itself doesn't even name Benjamin, Potiphar or Potiphar's wife.
So kulli shayʾ must be interpreted according to discourse/context: everything necessary/relevant to its revelatory guidance or subject matter, rather than an encyclopedia of all facts.
This is important whenever apologetic or polemical arguments quote:
The text itself constrains that reading.
Surah 12 — COMPLETE We have now completed 12:1–111.
12:1–3 Qur'an / Clear Book / Arabic revelation / Muhammad previously unaware
12:102 “This is from the reports of the unseen which We reveal to you”
12:103–110 Muhammad's mission / disbelief / signs / shirk / previous messengers / judgment
→ lesson → confirmation of what precedes → detailed exposition → guidance → mercy.
So Surah 12 does not present Joseph merely as ancient biography. The entire narrative is framed as evidence for revelation and continuity of prophecy.

Our historical comparison adds an essential second layer: many Qur'anic Joseph details absent from Genesis are demonstrably present in pre-Islamic Jewish and Christian interpretation, while several others still have no securely demonstrated pre-Islamic antecedent. That establishes a rich Late Antique traditional environment without, by itself, deciding the Qur'an's theological claim that the ultimate source is revelation.           Cambridge Univ…

Because this touches prophetic confidence in God's promises, it deserves a short textual/qirāʾāt investigation before we close Surah 12 completely.

And 12:3 is where this gets substantially more consequential for our project, because the Qur'an now says God is telling Muhammad “the best of stories” through revelation and that Muhammad was previously among those unaware of it. That statement gives us a historically testable question once the Joseph story begins: How closely does the supposedly previously unknown story follow Genesis, and where does it instead track Jewish or Christian extrabiblical traditions?
Surah 12:3 — “We relate to you the best of narratives”
Arabic ‫ِبَم ا َأْو َح ْيَن ا ِإَل ْيَك َٰهَذا اْلُق ْرآَن َو ِإن ُك نَت ِم ن َق ْبِلِه َل ِم َن اْل َغ اِفِل يَن‬   ‫َن ْح ُن َنُق ُّص َع َل ْيَك َأْح َس َن اْلَق َصِص‬
“We relate to you the best of narratives through what We have revealed to you in this Qur'an, although before it you were among those unaware.”
The early manuscript tradition confirms this wording; for example, Tübingen Ma VI 161 preserves 12:1–3 before beginning Joseph's dream at 12:4.                                   Corpus Coranicu…
This verse raises two separate questions that we should not blur together:
1. What does aḥsana al-qaṣaṣ mean? 2. What exactly does the Qur'an claim Muhammad did not previously know?
QB-0219: Still held—we haven't reached the first actual narrative comparison yet.

And now the setup is finished. 12:4 gives us our first hard comparison with Genesis: Joseph tells Jacob that he saw eleven stars, the sun and the moon prostrating to him. Genesis 37 contains essentially the same dream—but when we put the two texts side by side, several small differences immediately become worth investigating.
investigate the differences with Genesis side by side
Yes. Once Qur'an 12:4–5 is placed directly beside Genesis 37, the relationship is unmistakable—but so are several deliberate-looking narrative changes.
Joseph has two dreams                                   Yes                       Only one reported
First dream: brothers' sheaves bow to                   Yes                       Absent Joseph's sheaf
Celestial dream                                         Second dream              Only dream narrated
Joseph tells brothers                                   Yes                       No—he tells his father
Brothers already hear dream                             Yes                       Father tells Joseph not to tell them
Father's immediate reaction                             Rebukes Joseph            Protects/warns Joseph
Father interprets symbols aloud                         Yes                       Not explicitly
Brothers' jealousy connected directly to                Yes                       Qur'an develops jealousy separately in 12:8 dreams

The actual celestial image is extraordinarily close. Genesis says Joseph sees “the sun, the moon, and eleven stars” bowing to him; Qur'an 12:4 has eleven stars, the sun and moon prostrating to him. Sefaria +1
That deserves our first Surah 12 Bible-Qur'an record.
QB-0219 — Joseph's celestial dream Genesis 37:9: Joseph dreams that the sun, moon and eleven stars bow to him.                              Sefaria
Qur'an 12:4: Joseph sees eleven stars, the sun and moon prostrating to him.               Quranic Arabic …
Classification: STRONG PARALLEL This is not merely the generic motif “Joseph had a dream.” The constellation of details is highly specific:
The Qur'anic story clearly belongs to the same Joseph narrative tradition represented by Genesis 37.
But now the differences become more interesting.
Difference 1 — The Qur'an removes Joseph's first dream Genesis actually gives Joseph two dreams.
Dream 1 — Genesis 37:5–8 Joseph and his brothers are binding grain.
The brothers' sheaves surround it and bow to Joseph's sheaf.
His brothers immediately understand the implication:
Are you going to reign over us?
sun + moon + eleven stars → bow to Joseph.
The Qur'an completely omits the sheaf dream.
That is important because Genesis uses the two dreams together to intensify the conflict.
favoritism → hatred → dream #1 → more hatred → dream #2 → jealousy
celestial dream → Jacob warns Joseph → brothers' jealousy develops independently
So the Qur'an isn't simply abbreviating Genesis sentence by sentence. It is restructuring the narrative.
Difference 2 — Who hears the dream? This is probably the biggest narrative alteration.
Genesis Joseph tells his dreams to his brothers.
“He dreamed another dream and told it to his brothers…”
Only afterward does he also tell his father.                    Sefaria
Therefore the brothers already know about Joseph's predicted supremacy.
“My son, do not relate your vision to your brothers, lest they devise a plot against you.” Quranic Arabic …
That means the Qur'anic narrative apparently presupposes that the brothers have not heard the dream.
That is a genuine narrative difference.
QB-0219 — STRONG PARALLEL: Eleven stars + sun + moon bow/prostrate to Joseph.

QB-0220 — Who was told Joseph's dream? Genesis: Joseph tells the brothers.
Qur'an: Joseph tells his father, who explicitly tells him not to tell his brothers.
Classification: NARRATIVE DIFFERENCE — not necessarily contradiction about theology, but mutually different accounts of the event.
If we're asking historically what happened, both sequences cannot straightforwardly describe the same telling in the same way.
Difference 3 — Jacob's reaction is almost reversed This one is particularly striking.
“What is this dream you have dreamed?”
I = sun your mother = moon your brothers = eleven stars
and asks whether they are really going to bow before Joseph.                    Sefaria
“his father kept the matter in mind.”
So Jacob outwardly rebukes Joseph while apparently recognizing that the dream may be significant. Sefaria
Instead Jacob appears to recognize the danger immediately:
Don't tell your brothers or they'll plot against you.
God will choose you, teach you interpretation, and complete His favor upon you and Jacob's family. Quran
So Qur'anic Jacob understands Joseph's future significance much more explicitly.
Genesis Jacob: “What kind of dream is this?” → rebuke → privately remembers it.
Qur'anic Jacob: “I understand what this means—keep quiet because your brothers may plot against you.”
The Qur'an presents Jacob as possessing substantially greater prophetic insight.
Difference 4 — Satan enters the story Qur'an 12:5 adds something absent from Genesis:
“Indeed Satan is a manifest enemy to humanity.”                 Quranic Arabic …
Genesis attributes the brothers' behavior directly to human emotions:
hatred jealousy resentment over favoritism and Joseph's dreams.
It does not insert Satan into the Joseph narrative.
And this will return at the other end of the story.
In 12:100, Joseph says Satan had caused discord between him and his brothers.                     Altafsir.com
So Satan actually frames the Qur'anic Joseph narrative:
12:5 — Satan may provoke the brothers' plot
12:100 — Satan caused discord between Joseph and his brothers
That's a distinctly Qur'anic theological framing not present in Genesis.
QB-0220 — NARRATIVE DIFFERENCE: Genesis says Joseph tells the brothers; Qur'an has Jacob tell him not to tell them.
QB-0220 — UPDATED Genesis: Joseph voluntarily tells his brothers dreams depicting their submission to him.
Qur'an: Jacob specifically orders Joseph not to tell them.
Narrative consequence: Genesis allows Joseph's own behavior to contribute to escalating his brothers' resentment. Qur'anic Joseph does not provoke them with the dream.
App preservation: retain Genesis 37:5–11 ↔ Qur'an 12:4–5 and cross-link to the characterization record below.

records.title: Cause of the brothers' hostility
bodyParagraphs: Original heading/title: — Cause of the brothers' hostility
QB-0221 — Cause of the brothers' hostility Genesis: human favoritism, hatred and jealousy.
Qur'an: those human motives remain, but the narrative additionally places the conflict within Satanic antagonism.
Not a contradiction—the Qur'an could add an invisible cause Genesis doesn't mention—but it is clearly additional theology.
Difference 5 — There's a problem involving Joseph's mother Now we hit the most interesting difficulty.
Genesis tells us explicitly what the celestial symbols represent because Jacob says:
“Are we to come, I and your mother and your brothers, and bow low to you…?”         Sefaria
Sun = Jacob Moon = Joseph's mother 11 stars = brothers
But according to Genesis's own narrative chronology, Rachel—Joseph's mother—has already died.
Genesis 35 places Rachel's death while giving birth to Benjamin before the Joseph narrative of Genesis 37.
That creates an internal Genesis difficulty even before the Qur'an enters the picture:
How can Joseph's mother bow to him later if Rachel is already dead?
Jewish interpreters noticed exactly this problem.

One rabbinic solution identified the moon not with Rachel but with Bilhah, Rachel's handmaid, proposing that Bilhah raised Joseph like a mother. But, as modern analysis correctly notes, Genesis itself never says Bilhah raised Joseph as his mother and never records Bilhah bowing to Joseph. Later Nahmanides proposed a different symbolic solution.                      TheTorah.com
So this is an old interpretive problem, not something invented by Muslim-Christian polemics.
And the Qur'an may intensify that problem Jump temporarily to 12:100, because it explicitly tells us that Joseph's dream has been fulfilled.
raises his abawayhi onto the throne
“O my father, this is the interpretation of my former vision. My Lord has made it true.”         Altafsir.com
The Arabic ‫ — َأَبَو ْيِه‬abawayhi normally means his two parents.
Traditional Muslim interpretation therefore naturally understood:
Ibn Kathīr preserves precisely that interpretation.                Quran.com
But now we have the Genesis chronology problem:

Later Muslim interpreters consequently developed explanations, including identifying the woman as an aunt/stepmother rather than Rachel. One tafsīr tradition explicitly interprets the pair at 12:100 as Joseph's father and maternal aunt.                  Altafsir.com
That deserves a dedicated investigation when we reach 12:100.
QB-0221 — THEOLOGICAL DEVELOPMENT: Qur'an introduces Satan into the causal explanation of the family conflict; Genesis does not.
QB-0221 — UPDATED The Qur'an places the Joseph conflict within a cosmic moral framework:
Genesis explains the conflict entirely through the family narrative itself: favoritism, hatred, jealousy and Joseph's dreams.

Source-history question: Whether pre-Islamic Jewish or Christian Joseph traditions explicitly attributed the brothers' hostility to Satan should remain OPEN. If we find such a tradition, it becomes another chronologically testable extrabiblical parallel.
That should be preserved for the App rather than casually attributing this addition to the Qur'an alone before checking earlier literature.
Surah 12:6 — Jacob predicts Joseph's future Now Jacob says:

‫َو َكَٰذ ِلَك َيْج َت ِبيَك َر ُّبَك َو ُي َع ِّل ُم َك ِم ن َت ْأِو يِل ٱْلَأَح اِد يِث َو ُي ِتُّم ِنْع َم َت ُهۥ َع َل ْيَك َو َع َل ٰٓى َءاِل َيْع ُق وَب َكَم ٓا َأَتَّم َه ا َع َل ٰٓى َأَبَو ْيَك ِم ن َق ْبُل‬ ‫ِإْبَٰرِه يَم َو ِإْس َح ٰـَقۚ  ِإَّن َر َّبَك َع ِل يٌم َح ِك يٌم‬

“And thus your Lord will choose you, teach you something of the interpretation of al-aḥādīth, and complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Jacob, as He completed it previously upon your forefathers Abraham and Isaac. Indeed, your Lord is Knowing, Wise.”
There are several important differences with Genesis here.
QB-0221                 Qur'an introduces Satan into Joseph/brothers conflict;         Theological addition; source-history Genesis does not                                               OPEN
QB-0221 — Satanic causation now closes its arc At 12:5 Jacob warned:
do not tell your vision to your brothers lest they plot against you; Satan is an enemy.
“after Satan caused discord between me and my brothers.”
The Qur'an preserves those human causes and adds an invisible Satanic causal layer.
QB-0221 — FINAL Genesis: human family psychology.
Classification: BIBLICAL FAMILY CONFLICT + QUR'ANIC SATANIC CAUSAL ADDITION.
No secure pre-Islamic Joseph-specific Satan parallel established in our investigation.
12:101 — Joseph's final prayer Joseph now prays:
‫َرِّب َق ْد آَت ْي َت ِني ِم َن اْل ُم ْلِك َو َع َّل ْم َت ِني ِم ن َت ْأِو يِل اْلَأَح اِد يِث‬
“My Lord, You have given me something of sovereignty and taught me something of the taʾwīl of events/dreams…”
“You are my protector in this world and the Hereafter.”
“Cause me to die as a muslim and join me with the righteous.”

records.title: Who is the “moon”?
bodyParagraphs: QB-0222 — Who is the “moon”? Genesis 37: Jacob explicitly says “your mother,” even though Genesis has already narrated Rachel's death.
Qur'an 12: leaves the symbols uninterpreted at 12:4 but eventually says Joseph's abawayhi participate in the fulfillment at 12:100.
Jewish interpretation: already wrestled with the dead-Rachel problem and generated alternative identifications such as Bilhah.             TheTorah.com
Islamic interpretation: likewise generated alternative solutions.
STATUS: OPEN — investigate pre-Islamic Jewish traditions before deciding whether the Qur'an reflects one.
This one could become extremely important for our source-history project.
Difference 6 — Joseph's personality changes Genesis's Joseph is seventeen when introduced and is not portrayed entirely sympathetically.
reports negatively about his brothers, is visibly his father's favorite, receives special clothing, and voluntarily tells his brothers dreams implying his supremacy.
The brothers' behavior becomes horrific, but Genesis gives us psychological reasons for the family conflict before they commit their crime.                   Sefaria
The Qur'an strips much of that away.
No special coat at the beginning.
No Joseph telling his brothers that they will bow before him.
Joseph privately tells his father → father warns him → brothers become jealous independently.
That makes Qur'anic Joseph appear considerably less provocative and more innocent at the outset.
That's a literary/theological difference worth tracking.
And here's the major structural discovery The Qur'an hasn't simply copied Genesis 37 and shortened it.

Genesis causal chain Jacob favors Joseph → special garment → brothers hate Joseph → Joseph reports dream #1 to them → hatred increases → Joseph reports dream #2 → brothers become jealous → Jacob rebukes Joseph → later brothers plot against him.

Qur'anic causal chain Joseph receives celestial dream → tells Jacob privately → Jacob recognizes divine significance → warns Joseph not to tell brothers → Satan could exploit their hostility → God will choose Joseph → brothers independently resent Jacob's preference → brothers plot against Joseph.
That changes the moral center of the story.
The Qur'an emphasizes divine election versus human jealousy, with Satan operating behind the conflict.
Both ultimately tell the same recognizable Joseph story, but they tell it for somewhat different theological purposes.

QB-0222 — OPEN SOURCE-HISTORY PROBLEM: The moon/mother problem. Rachel's prior death creates interpretive difficulty already within Genesis; both Jewish and Islamic traditions subsequently attempt solutions. We need to determine how early the Jewish Bilhah solution actually is before considering whether it could have influenced the Qur'anic tradition.
QB-0222 — Rachel, Bilhah, and Joseph's dream 1. The problem originates inside Genesis The sequence is straightforward.
Genesis 35:19: Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin.
Then in Genesis 37:9–10, Joseph dreams that the sun, moon and eleven stars bow before him. Jacob interprets the imagery:
“I and your mother and your brothers…”
The obvious problem was therefore visible to any careful ancient reader:
Rachel is already dead. How can Joseph's mother later bow before him?
This isn't a Qur'an-created problem. Ancient Jewish and Christian interpreters noticed it independently.
2. We can prove Jews were discussing the problem centuries before Islam This is stronger than Genesis Rabbah alone.

Origen — third century CE Origen, writing in the third century, explicitly says that Rachel had already died and reports a Jewish explanation of the difficulty: according to “some Jews,” Rachel would be resurrected so that the dream could eventually be fulfilled.

Maren Niehoff's study of Origen and Genesis Rabbah points out that Origen is independently witnessing a Jewish interpretation of exactly this textual problem around the middle of the third century CE. Scribd
Jewish interpretive problem already circulating by c. third century
So there is no question anymore whether Jews noticed Rachel's death only after Islam.
They demonstrably noticed it centuries beforehand.
3. Genesis Rabbah gives two solutions Now we get the particularly relevant evidence.
Genesis Rabbah 84:11 preserves a discussion attributed to Rabbi Levi in the name of Rabbi Ḥama bar Ḥanina.
Rachel is dead, yet Jacob speaks about Joseph's “mother” bowing.
One interpretation supposes that Jacob expected resurrection of the dead during his lifetime.
Jacob did not realize that the dream referred to Bilhah, Rachel's maidservant, who raised Joseph like a mother.          Sefaria +1
That is precisely the possibility we were looking for.
4. How early is the Bilhah interpretation? Here's where we need our chronology controls.

Genesis Rabbah as a collection is generally dated to the early fifth century, roughly 400–450 CE, in Roman Palestine. Modern scholarship describes it as the earliest rabbinic commentary on Genesis. Mohr Siebeck +1

Moreover, the tradition is attributed to Palestinian amoraic figures from considerably earlier. Rabbi Ḥama bar Ḥanina is placed around 260 CE, while Rabbi Levi belongs to the third-century Palestinian amoraic world.        Mohr Siebeck +1
That sounds spectacular—but we need one caution.

Genesis Rabbah 84 has redactional complications. Scholarship has identified material in chapter 84, among several other portions, as containing later additions or expansions. Consequently, we cannot simply reason:
Rabbi Levi lived in the third century → therefore every word attributed to him in Genesis Rabbah 84:11 was written in the third century.
That's not historically safe.           Kiwix Server +1
Nevertheless, even using the conservative dating of the literary collection, the Bilhah interpretation belongs to a Late Antique Jewish exegetical tradition whose literary setting predates Islam.
So our evidence grades should be:
Jewish awareness of Rachel problem before Islam: CERTAIN.
Bilhah solution attested in Genesis Rabbah: CERTAIN.
Exact Bilhah wording demonstrably fixed by c. 260: NOT PROVABLE.

Bilhah interpretation existing before the seventh-century Qur'an: strongly supported, but because of chapter 84's redaction history I would avoid calling the exact wording absolutely datable to the third century.
5. Targum Neofiti gives us an interesting control I checked the Palestinian Aramaic Targum tradition as well.

Targum Neofiti's Genesis 37 follows the biblical sequence closely: Joseph dreams that the sun, moon and eleven stars salute/bow to him, tells the brothers, and then tells his father. It does not, in the material located, solve the problem by inserting Bilhah directly into Genesis 37:9–10.             Betemunah
The Bilhah solution was a Jewish exegetical tradition, not simply a variant biblical text replacing Rachel with Bilhah.
The Qur'an therefore isn't following an alternative Genesis manuscript that simply said “Bilhah.”
6. Now compare the Qur'an This is where things get really interesting.
Then at the end of the story:
Joseph raises his abawayhi onto the throne, and they fall/prostrate before him.
“O my father, this is the interpretation of my earlier vision…”
And now we have exactly the Genesis problem again.
7. But the Qur'an never identifies the woman This is crucial.
In fact, the Qur'an's Joseph narrative doesn't name Joseph's mother at all.
“The Qur'an says Bilhah was Joseph's mother.”
“The Qur'an copied Genesis Rabbah's Bilhah solution.”
What we can say is much more interesting:
The Qur'an tells the same celestial dream while avoiding Genesis 37:10's explicit identification of the moon as Joseph's biological mother.
Then at fulfillment it uses abawayhi, without identifying the female parent figure.
That leaves room for exactly the sort of surrogate-parent solution found in Jewish interpretation.
8. And early Islamic tradition noticed the same problem Later Islamic historiography/exegesis shows disagreement over precisely who the second parent in 12:100 was.
Jacob + Joseph's aunt, because Rachel had already died.                   Emaan Library

Other Islamic traditions even propose that God resurrected Rachel so that Joseph's dream could be fulfilled—the same broad solution to the textual problem that Origen already reports from Jews centuries before Islam.            Scribd
Genesis                                                         Rachel apparently represented, despite having died
Jewish interpretation known to Origen, 3rd c.                   Rachel resurrected
Genesis Rabbah                                                  Rachel problem explicitly recognized
Genesis Rabbah                                                  Bilhah as surrogate mother
Qur'an, 7th c.                                                  Dream retained; woman not identified by name
Islamic interpretation                                          Rachel / aunt / alternative maternal figure
That is exactly the kind of chronology-sensitive comparison our project was designed to detect.
9. Does this prove Qur'anic dependence on Genesis Rabbah? No.
There are at least four historically possible models:
Direct literary dependence: Qur'anic material derives from Genesis Rabbah or a related text.
Oral Jewish tradition: the same interpretation circulated orally in Late Antique Jewish communities and reached the Qur'anic environment without direct textual borrowing.
Shared interpretive environment: Jewish, Christian and Qur'anic storytellers were independently wrestling with the same obvious Genesis problem.
Independent Qur'anic retelling: the Qur'an simply omits the mother's identity for its own narrative purposes; later Muslims independently encounter the same problem.
Our evidence cannot presently choose among those possibilities.
But we can eliminate one claim:
“There was no pre-Islamic Jewish tradition dealing with this issue.”
10. There's an even older Christian witness to the Jewish debate Origen makes the source-history case stronger because he is not a medieval Jewish source retrojected backward.
He's a third-century Christian writer reporting what Jews were saying about Genesis.
And importantly, the Jewish interpretation he reports isn't the Bilhah solution—it is the resurrection solution.

Genesis Rabbah subsequently knows both the resurrection problem/solution and the Bilhah solution. Niehoff argues that this shows an active Jewish exegetical conversation surrounding this precise difficulty in Late Antiquity.          Scribd
Joseph's dead-mother problem was already an established exegetical puzzle hundreds of years before Muhammad. That's the historically important finding.
QB-0222 — UPDATED RECORD Biblical datum Genesis 35:19 says Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin.
Genesis 37:9–10 subsequently has Joseph dream of sun + moon + eleven stars, and Jacob interprets them as himself + Joseph's mother + brothers.
By the third century, Origen independently witnesses Jews addressing the problem through Rachel's future resurrection.            Scribd

Genesis Rabbah 84:11 explicitly recognizes Rachel's death and preserves the alternative interpretation that the dream's maternal figure is Bilhah, Rachel's maidservant, who raised Joseph as a mother. The collection is generally placed in fifth-century Roman Palestine, though chapter 84's redactional complexity prevents us from automatically dating every formulation to its attributed third-century rabbi. but does not identify the celestial figures.

Later Islamic evidence Muslim interpreters themselves disagreed over whether the woman was Rachel or another maternal relative/figure, and some Islamic material even uses the resurrection-of-Rachel solution known from earlier Jewish interpretation.             Emaan Library +1
DIRECT QUR'AN ↔ GENESIS RABBAH DEPENDENCE: NOT DEMONSTRATED.
ORAL/TRADITIONAL CONTACT: HISTORICALLY POSSIBLE; NOT PROVEN.
The most precise conclusion is therefore:

Surah 12 participates in a Joseph narrative environment in which an interpretive problem demonstrably discussed by Jews centuries before Islam—the dead mother in Joseph's dream—is left strategically unnamed rather than explicitly resolved. Later Islamic interpreters then reproduce solutions strikingly similar to pre-Islamic Jewish solutions.
That is stronger than a vague “Qur'an resembles Jewish tradition” claim because we can actually establish the chronology.

For now we can safely proceed to 12:5–6, where Jacob's warning and his prediction that God will teach Joseph “the interpretation of narratives/events” (taʾwīl al-aḥādīth) gives us our next comparison with Genesis—and another potential extrabiblical development.

QB-0227 — Reuben/Judah compression investigation First establish the Genesis baseline:
Genesis 37 Reuben → hears murder plan → says don't kill Joseph → proposes putting him in the pit → secretly intends to rescue him.
Judah → sees the Ishmaelite caravan → says don't kill Joseph → proposes selling him → brothers agree.

Then Genesis becomes textually difficult because Midianites appear and Joseph is removed from the pit, while other verses identify the purchasers/carriers as Ishmaelites. This complexity is one major reason modern source critics often identify intertwined Reuben/Midianite and Judah/Ishmaelite narrative strands.           TheTorah.com +1
“One of them said: Do not kill Joseph, but cast him into the hidden depth of the well; some travelers will pick him up…”
That anonymous speaker possesses elements of both Genesis sequences:
Reuben: don't kill + pit Judah episode: removal through passing travelers.
Now let's see whether that combination already existed before Islam.

1. Book of Jubilees — second century BCE This is our strongest securely pre-Islamic control because Jubilees is unquestionably ancient Jewish rewritten Scripture. Oxford describes it as a Jewish work from the second century BCE, and Hebrew copies among the Dead Sea Scrolls confirm its antiquity.                 OUP Academic +1
And Jubilees does something remarkable to Genesis 37.
Jubilees 34:11 Instead of recounting Reuben's intervention and then Judah's proposal, it summarizes:
Joseph's brothers plotted to kill him, changed their minds, and sold him to Ishmaelite merchants. Christian Classic…
The whole tangled Genesis sequence has become:
sell Joseph to passing Ishmaelite merchants
Finding By approximately the second century BCE, Jewish retellers were already willing to compress and rewrite Genesis's complicated Reuben/Judah/Midianite/Ishmaelite sequence.
So the Qur'an's streamlined account cannot automatically be explained as an innovation originating in the seventh century.
2. Josephus — first century CE Josephus gives us an excellent counterexample because he does the opposite.
Writing in the first century CE, Josephus preserves the distinction very clearly.
Reuben Josephus has Reuben oppose murder and persuade the brothers to place Joseph in a dry pit. Reuben then leaves.
Judah After Reuben leaves, Judah sees the passing Ishmaelite/Arab merchants and proposes:
pull Joseph out → sell him to the merchants.
Reuben later returns intending secretly to rescue Joseph and discovers that he is gone.   Penelope +1
That is basically Genesis's division of roles, although Josephus smooths some of Genesis's narrative difficulties.
Significance There was clearly no single standardized Second Temple retelling.
Different Jewish writers handled Genesis differently.
3. Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs — even more interesting Now we encounter a fascinating tradition—but its dating requires caution.

The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs contains ancient Jewish material but survives in a Christian textual form. Scholarship remains divided about its compositional history. Some scholars defend a largely Hasmonean Jewish origin with Christian interpolation; others understand its extant form as a second- century CE Christian composition using older Jewish traditions. Either way, the material is pre-Islamic, but we should not automatically label every passage “Second Temple Jewish.”               OUP Academic +1
And this work radically redistributes the Joseph episode.
Testament of Zebulun Here Zebulun himself says that when the brothers wanted to kill Joseph, he pleaded with them not to commit the crime.
Reuben arose and said, “My brothers, let us not kill him, but let us cast him into one of these dry pits…”         New Advent +1
Already this is much more elaborate than Genesis.
And notice something relevant to the Qur'an:
The pit is specifically said to be dry, and providence has arranged it so Joseph will survive until he can be sold to the Ishmaelites.            New Advent
That is conceptually closer to the Qur'an's:
put him in the jubb so travelers can retrieve him
than merely throwing him somewhere to die.
But the speaker is still explicitly Reuben, not anonymous.
4. Testament of Gad changes responsibility again This gets even stranger.
The Testament of Gad says Gad wanted Joseph dead because of hatred and jealousy.
But its textual witnesses differ over the sale.
Judah sold him secretly to the Ishmaelites.               B4Bible +1
And another manuscript tradition apparently associates Gad and Simeon with the sale.          New Advent +1
That textual instability itself is informative.
The identity and precise responsibility of individual brothers were fluid within the extrabiblical Joseph tradition.
was already something ancient retellings could modify.
5. Genesis Rabbah Genesis Rabbah, broadly a fifth-century Palestinian Jewish work, also wrestles with Reuben's disappearance during Joseph's sale.
One explanation says Reuben was away serving his father.
Another says he had withdrawn in sackcloth and fasting, repenting for his earlier offense involving Bilhah. Sefaria +1
Genesis Rabbah therefore retains Reuben but supplies information Genesis itself doesn't provide to explain why he wasn't present when Joseph disappeared.
the ancient Jewish tradition is actively repairing narrative gaps in Genesis 37.

That produces a much stronger historical picture.
Does the Qur'an simply combine Reuben and Judah? Our earlier hypothesis was:
Qur'an's anonymous brother = compressed Reuben + Judah.
I would now downgrade that wording.

Hundreds of years before Islam, it had already removed both Reuben's and Judah's names and compressed their complicated interventions into a collective decision by the brothers.    Christian Classic… +1

Pre-Islamic evidence Jubilees (2nd c. BCE): compresses the sequence dramatically, omitting Reuben and Judah as individual actors and portraying the brothers collectively as changing their minds and selling Joseph to Ishmaelite merchants.             Christian Classic… +1

And this gives our App/database an important methodological category we should preserve:

It means we can demonstrate that a biblical narrative was already being rewritten in multiple ways before Islam, but we cannot identify which particular version—written or oral—lies behind the Qur'anic form.
That distinction will keep us from making the common mistake of saying “the Qur'an copied Midrash X” merely because Midrash X resembles it.

QB-0227 can now be closed as an investigation while remaining cross-linked to QB-0229. And QB- 0229 may be even more revealing when we reach 12:19–20, because that's where we can test whether the Qur'an also smooths Genesis's notorious Midianites ↔ Ishmaelites ↔ brothers problem in a way already found in pre-Islamic Joseph retellings.

Continuing with Surah 12:11–14. These verses cover the brothers persuading Jacob to let Joseph accompany them, and they expose another interesting difference in how Genesis and the Qur'an portray Jacob's foreknowledge of danger.
Surah 12:11–12 — “Why don't you trust us with Joseph?” The brothers say:
“O our father, why do you not trust us with Joseph, when indeed we are sincere toward him? Send him with us tomorrow so that he may enjoy himself and play, and surely we will guard him.”
The Arabic ‫ — َت ْأَم َّن ا‬taʾmannā concerns trusting/entrusting Joseph to them.
So the Qur'an makes something explicit:
Jacob already does not trust the brothers with Joseph.
That follows naturally from 12:5, where Jacob warned Joseph not to reveal his dream because the brothers might plot against him.
The Qur'anic narrative therefore creates a continuous thread:
12:5: Jacob anticipates danger from brothers ↓ 12:11: brothers recognize Jacob doesn't trust them ↓ 12:12: they promise protection.

records.title: The wolf
bodyParagraphs: QB-0231 — The wolf Here's a major Qur'an–Genesis difference.
Qur'an Jacob himself introduces the wolf before anything happens.
Later, in 12:17, the brothers return claiming:
So they appropriate Jacob's own stated fear.
Genesis The brothers do not claim a wolf specifically.
After dipping Joseph's garment in goat blood, they show it to Jacob.
The Hebrew is essentially ḥayyāh rāʿāh:
Genesis Brothers provide bloody garment ↓ Jacob concludes wild animal killed Joseph.
Qur'an Jacob first suggests wolf danger ↓ brothers later use Jacob's fear as their fabricated explanation.
QB-0231 — NEW Genesis: Jacob independently concludes from the bloody garment that a wild animal killed Joseph.
Qur'an: Jacob mentions a wolf beforehand, and the brothers subsequently appropriate that exact scenario.
We should eventually investigate whether a pre-Islamic Jewish Joseph tradition specifically identified the animal as a wolf.
If it did, that would be another extrabiblical parallel.

QB-0231                 Genesis: Jacob infers a wild animal attack afterward;         Narrative development; source-history Qur'an: Jacob specifically fears a wolf beforehand,           OPEN which becomes the brothers' lie
QB-0231 — The wolf investigation 1. Hebrew Bible baseline Genesis actually uses the “wild beast” idea twice.
Before the brothers act, they themselves propose the future deception:
Genesis 37:20: they will claim that a ḥayyāh rāʿāh, literally an “evil/wild animal,” ate Joseph.
Then after receiving the bloody garment:
Genesis 37:33: Jacob concludes that a ḥayyāh rāʿāh devoured Joseph.
So I need to refine our previous record slightly.
Genesis does contain the animal explanation before Joseph's disappearance—but it comes from the brothers planning their lie, not from Jacob.
Genesis Brothers: “We'll say a wild animal ate him.”
Qur'an Jacob: “I fear a wolf may eat him.”
That is almost an elegant reversal of speakers.
This is stronger than what we recorded previously.
2. Jubilees — second century BCE Our earliest major Jewish rewritten-Bible witness does not produce the Qur'anic wolf.
brothers plot against Joseph → change their minds → sell him → slaughter a goat → stain Joseph's garment → send it to Jacob.
a wild animal had eaten Joseph.                  Palimpsest Project
So Jubilees preserves the generic Genesis animal.
Jacob does not predict an animal attack beforehand.
Result Jubilees ≠ Qur'an on this detail.
3. Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs This corpus certainly knows wolves in the Joseph-family setting.
For example, the Testament of Gad describes Gad defending the family flocks against:
lion, wolf, leopard, bear and other wild beasts.                Christian Classic…
So wolves are completely natural within the pastoral world of these traditions.
Jacob predicts the wolf before Joseph leaves.
I have not found that in the pre-Islamic Testaments material.
Therefore it cannot currently serve as the source parallel we're looking for.
4. Genesis Rabbah — crucial negative result This is where I expected the best chance of finding it.
Genesis Rabbah is exactly the kind of Late Antique Jewish exegetical corpus where Genesis's anonymous “wild beast” could have become a specific animal.
But the scholarship addressing this exact Qur'anic problem reports:
no rabbinic source has been identified that specifies a wolf in Joseph's supposed death.
Joseph Witztum's study of the Qur'an's Syriac/Jewish milieu explicitly notes this absence while discussing Q 12.        Scribd

Another specialized study of Surah Yusuf reaches essentially the same result: identifying an unspecified biblical entity with a specific one is certainly a familiar rabbinic interpretive technique, but there is no
known rabbinic text actually identifying Genesis's “bad/wild animal” as a wolf in this episode. Scribd +1
“The Qur'an's wolf comes from Genesis Rabbah.”
The evidence currently doesn't support it.
5. Targumic tradition doesn't give us the Qur'anic wolf either The Palestinian Aramaic tradition adds many details to Joseph's story, but the evidence I located does not supply our missing link.
In fact, Targum Pseudo-Jonathan makes an extraordinary alteration at Genesis 37:33.

Rather than simply having Jacob conclude that a beast killed Joseph, it portrays Jacob as perceiving through the Holy Spirit that Joseph has not been devoured by a beast or killed by a man, but that an evil woman will confront him—foreshadowing Potiphar's wife.                     Scribd
That's fascinating for our larger project because it shows just how freely Jewish interpretive traditions could transform this verse.
6. The wolf definitely appears in later Jewish tradition Now things change.
The medieval Sefer ha-Yashar tradition contains an elaborate wolf episode.
After the brothers claim Joseph was devoured, Jacob orders them to find the animal.

And the wolf miraculously speaks, denying that it killed Joseph and explaining that it is searching for its own lost cub. The Jewish Encyclopedia summarizes precisely this tradition.                Jewish Encyclop… +1
That is obviously much closer to later Islamic Joseph lore.
But chronology kills its value as evidence for Qur'anic dependence:
Sefer ha-Yashar in this form is post-Qur'anic.

The specialized scholarship explicitly warns about this: the talking-wolf material occurs in a work composed centuries after the Qur'an, and similar expanded wolf stories also occur in post-Qur'anic Islamic literature.         Scribd
later Jewish wolf story ≠ evidence for Qur'anic borrowing.
We must preserve that distinction in the App.
7. What about pre-Islamic Christianity/Syriac tradition? I specifically checked the Syriac/Christian avenue because this would be an obvious place for a missing intermediary.
I found plenty of Christian wolf imagery and Joseph typology, including Syriac material, but not the required narrative sequence:
Jacob → Joseph → predicted wolf → brothers later use wolf story.
Pre-Islamic Jewish wolf identification: not demonstrated.
Pre-Islamic Christian/Syriac wolf identification: not demonstrated.
Pre-Islamic Jacob predicting wolf: not found.
That's a meaningful negative result—but it must be phrased as:
8. But why a wolf? There is one intriguing biblical possibility.
Genesis itself associates one of Jacob's sons with a wolf:
Rabbinic interpretation certainly knew and developed that wolf symbolism; Genesis Rabbah, for example, interprets Benjamin explicitly through the wolf image.                Sefaria +1
Could that somehow have influenced the Joseph story?
Possible—but there is zero evidence presently connecting Genesis 49:27's Benjamin-wolf to Qur'an 12:13's wolf.
So we should not turn an interesting association into a source claim.
9. The Qur'an has done something more interesting than simply replacing “animal” with “wolf” This is the key finding.
generic biblical animal → specific Qur'anic wolf.
But that's not all it does.
It reorganizes who invents the animal story.
“Let's claim a wild animal ate him.”
“I fear a wolf will eat him.”
The brothers use their father's own fear against him.
That feature is not present in Genesis.
Nor have we located it in our pre-Islamic comparative sources.
QB-0231 — UPDATED PERMANENT RECORD Biblical baseline Genesis 37:20 has the brothers themselves anticipate claiming that a generic wild animal devoured Joseph.
Genesis 37:33 has Jacob subsequently infer the same explanation from Joseph's bloody garment.
Second Temple evidence Jubilees 34: preserves the generic wild animal explanation and does not have Jacob predict it beforehand.          Palimpsest Project

Other pre-Islamic Jewish/Christian evidence The Testaments knows wolves in the brothers' pastoral environment but does not provide the Qur'anic sequence located so far.                  Christian Classic…
Known rabbinic material has not yielded a wolf identification for Genesis 37's wild animal. Specialized scholarship explicitly notes this absence.                 Scribd +1
No demonstrable pre-Islamic Syriac/Christian example of Jacob predicting a wolf was located in this investigation.

Later Jewish evidence Sefer ha-Yashar develops an elaborate talking-wolf narrative, but it is post-Qur'anic and therefore cannot establish a pre-Islamic source for Q 12.                        Jewish Encyclop… +1
Jacob: “I fear the wolf will eat him.”
GENERIC WILD ANIMAL → WOLF: Qur'anic specification; no securely demonstrated pre-Islamic source located.
JACOB PREDICTS THE WOLF BEFOREHAND: no pre-Islamic parallel located.
LOST ORAL TRADITION: possible but unevidenced.
SOURCE-HISTORY STATUS: OPEN, with negative evidence recorded.

This is actually a valuable result for our eventual App because we shouldn't only preserve matches. We need records where a proposed Jewish or Christian source was actively searched for and not found. Otherwise the database would create a false impression that every Qur'anic departure from Genesis can be traced to an earlier Jewish or Christian text.

We can now advance into 12:15–18 with this resolved provisionally. That passage gives us the pit revelation, the bloody shirt, the brothers' false crying, and Jacob's refusal to believe them—and the bloody-shirt episode has especially strong potential because it lets us test the Qur'an against Genesis, Jubilees, the Testaments, and Late Antique Jewish interpretation simultaneously.

Continuing with Surah 12:15–18. This section contains four elements we need to separate carefully: revelation to Joseph in the pit, the brothers' staged crying, the bloody shirt, and Jacob's response.

“to put him in the hidden depth of the well/cistern.”

and then dipped it in goat blood.

blood + intact garment → therefore no animal attack

if Joseph had been devoured, the tunic would have been torn apart.

Jacob observes that there are no:

with the precise dating/authorship qualification attached.

The scholarly notes accompanying the text also point out that Jacob's doubt appears in the Palestinian Targum, Romanos, Genizah fragments, and Genesis Rabbah-related tradition.                 Exegpatrpicasaco
So we're no longer dealing with an isolated Muslim motif.

Instead Jacob perceives through divine/holy inspiration that an evil woman will threaten Joseph later— again pointing toward Potiphar's wife.                  Scribd

the much earlier authorities to whom reports are attributed.

they brought Joseph's shirt with false blood.

records.title: Joseph discovered through the water vessel

bodyParagraphs: Original heading/title: — Joseph discovered through the water vessel
QB-0241 — Joseph discovered through the water vessel
Let's establish the biblical baseline first.
1. Genesis does NOT contain the bucket discovery Genesis 37:24 explicitly says:
the pit was empty; there was no water in it.
Then the brothers see the caravan.
a traveler approaches looking for water, someone lowers a bucket, Joseph is discovered while drawing water, or Joseph comes up with the water vessel.
Joseph's removal occurs in the difficult Genesis 37:28 sequence involving the Midianite traders/Ishmaelites.
So the Qur'anic bucket scene is not simply Genesis 37 rewritten more concisely.
2. Josephus does not supply it Josephus, writing in the first century CE, smooths Genesis but retains essentially:
brothers put Joseph in pit → merchants appear → Judah proposes sale → Joseph is taken from pit → sold.
There is no independent water-drawer discovering Joseph.
3. Jubilees doesn't supply it either Jubilees also simplifies Genesis substantially.
brothers decide against killing Joseph → sell him to Ishmaelite merchants.
Therefore our major Second Temple rewritten-Bible witness does not explain Qur'an 12:19.
4. But Genesis Rabbah does This is where the investigation becomes significant.

Genesis Rabbah, the Late Antique Palestinian Jewish midrash compiled broadly around the fifth century CE, preserves a tradition connected with Joseph's removal from the pit in which the merchants approach the pit for water.
The tradition explains the biblical statement about the pit containing no water and develops the circumstances of Joseph's discovery/removal beyond Genesis itself.
This is precisely the kind of chronological evidence we were looking for:
→ Joseph's pit becomes associated with travelers/merchants seeking water.
The connection between Joseph's discovery and water-seeking existed before the Qur'an.
But there's an even closer witness.
5. Targumic Joseph tradition gets much closer Palestinian Aramaic retellings of Genesis expand the merchant episode substantially.
In the expanded Targumic tradition, the travelers approach the pit in connection with obtaining water and Joseph's presence becomes known through the attempt to draw from it.
That is dramatically closer to Qur'an 12:19 than canonical Genesis.
So the shared expanded structure becomes:
Genesis Joseph in empty pit → merchants appear → Joseph removed/sold.
Palestinian Jewish expansion Joseph in pit → travelers/merchants interact with pit as a water source → Joseph is discovered/removed.
Qur'an Joseph in jubb → caravan arrives → sends water-drawer → bucket lowered → Joseph discovered.
That is a genuine extrabiblical parallel.
6. But dating the Targums requires caution This is exactly where our chronology rule matters.

The surviving forms of Palestinian Targumic works such as Targum Pseudo-Jonathan are textually complicated and contain material from multiple periods, including material that may have reached final form after Islam.
Instead we ask whether the motif is independently anchored in pre-Islamic Jewish interpretation.
And Genesis Rabbah provides that anchor for the water-seeking component.
Secure conclusion Water-seeking at Joseph's pit: PRE-ISLAMIC JEWISH PARALLEL — CONFIRMED.

Stronger exact conclusion lowering a bucket and discovering Joseph: attested in expanded Jewish/Targumic tradition, but the exact textual witness must be dated carefully before claiming that every detail is demonstrably pre-Islamic.
That's the distinction we need in the database.
7. The Syriac Christian tradition strengthens the picture The expanded Joseph tradition was also extremely popular in Syriac Christianity.
Late Antique Syriac Joseph literature contains extensive embellishment of the pit episode and the merchants' discovery of Joseph.
This matters because we have already found that Syriac Joseph tradition preserved the untorn-garment inference absent from Genesis.
So we're seeing a broader pattern:
Surah 12 repeatedly resembles the Late Antique expanded Joseph narrative environment, not merely the bare Genesis text.
But again, we should not turn that observation into:
Different Jewish and Christian traditions circulated, interacted and were transmitted orally as well as textually.
Our evidence supports traditional environment, not a uniquely identifiable document.
8. There is an even more interesting narrative consequence Remember Genesis says:
there was no water in the pit.
That creates an obvious interpretive opportunity.
Imagine travelers approaching what they believe is a cistern.
The Qur'an uses exactly that dramatic mechanism.
and receives something far more valuable:
So Qur'an 12:19 isn't contradicting Genesis's “no water” statement.
Ironically, the absence of water can actually make the expanded tradition work:
That may explain why the motif naturally arose in Jewish retelling.
9. And this affects QB-0239 We previously recorded:
Genesis says no water; Qur'an has water-drawer.
There is no contradiction at all required.
It says the traveler lowered his bucket.
he expected water and instead found Joseph.
QB-0241 — PERMANENT RECORD Title Joseph Discovered Through Water-Seeking at the Pit
Joseph placed in an empty cistern with no water.
Passing merchants subsequently become involved in his removal/sale.
No water-drawer or bucket discovery appears in the canonical text.
Second Temple Jewish evidence Jubilees: no bucket/water-drawer discovery.
Therefore the motif is not demonstrated in those early witnesses.
Late Antique Jewish evidence Palestinian Jewish interpretation develops the merchants' encounter with Joseph's pit in connection with seeking water.
Genesis Rabbah provides a pre-Islamic chronological anchor for the water-seeking development.

Expanded Palestinian Aramaic/Targumic traditions move closer still toward a water-drawing discovery, although exact individual textual forms require careful dating because surviving Targumic compositions are layered.
Classification GENESIS DIRECT PARALLEL: basic pit + travelers only.
EXACT BUCKET-DISCOVERY PARALLEL: STRONG TRADITIONAL PARALLEL, but exact witness chronology must remain qualified.
DIRECT QUR'AN ↔ GENESIS RABBAH DEPENDENCE: NOT DEMONSTRATED.
DIRECT QUR'AN ↔ TARGUM DEPENDENCE: NOT DEMONSTRATED.
QB-0241 becomes one of the strongest extrabiblical parallels we've found in Surah 12.
I tightened the claim, and the result requires a correction to my previous answer:
I cannot currently verify the exact “water-drawer lowers a bucket and thereby discovers Joseph” mechanism in a securely datable pre-Islamic Jewish or Christian witness.
The broader water/pit tradition is ancient. The exact Qur'anic bucket-discovery sequence is not yet securely demonstrated before the Qur'an.
1. What Genesis actually gives us Genesis 37:24:
the pit was empty; there was no water in it.
Genesis 37:25–28 then introduces the caravan and Joseph's removal.
no water-drawer, no lowered bucket, and no accidental discovery of Joseph while seeking water.
So the exact Qur'anic mechanism remains extrabiblical.
2. Jubilees — securely pre-Islamic, but no bucket Jubilees is extremely early—second century BCE—and therefore an excellent control.
But it simply has the brothers change their minds and sell Joseph to Ishmaelite merchants.
3. Josephus — securely pre-Islamic, but no bucket Josephus likewise knows the pit and passing merchants but doesn't give us the Qur'anic discovery mechanism.
These two witnesses matter because they show that the bucket episode was not an inevitable early development of Genesis 37.
4. Genesis Rabbah needs correction This is where my previous response went too far.
“Genesis Rabbah provides a pre-Islamic chronological anchor for the water-seeking development.”
That statement was too confident for the exact claim we're testing.

Genesis Rabbah is certainly pre-Islamic in broad redactional terms—generally associated with Roman Palestine in Late Antiquity—but I have not verified an exact passage in Genesis Rabbah containing the Qur'anic mechanism:
merchants arrive seeking water → lower bucket → discover Joseph.
Therefore we should not use Genesis Rabbah as proof of the bucket-discovery motif.
That part of QB-0241 needs to be downgraded.
5. The Palestinian Targums are the real problem This is where closely related expanded material appears.
But we have exactly the chronological problem you anticipated.

Targum Pseudo-Jonathan It contains ancient traditions but its final composition/redaction is generally regarded as considerably later and includes material demonstrating that its surviving form cannot simply be assigned wholesale to pre-Islamic antiquity.
A close parallel in Pseudo-Jonathan does not prove that the parallel existed before the Qur'an.
the same motif quoted/attested by an identifiable pre-Islamic author.
I have not established either for the exact bucket-discovery mechanism.

6. What about Syriac Christianity? This was the most promising alternative because Syriac Joseph literature clearly preserves other pre- Islamic expansions—we just demonstrated that with the untorn garment.
But for this specific detail I have not found a securely dated Ephremic, Narsai, Jacob of Serugh, Romanos, or comparable pre-Islamic Christian witness that unmistakably gives:
Joseph is discovered through the bucket.
There are expanded pit and merchant traditions, but that's insufficient for our standard.
A source must actually contain the mechanism we're testing.
7. Therefore the evidentiary ladder changes We should now distinguish three things.
Level A — Pit + passing merchants Definitely pre-Islamic.
Level B — Expanded traditions surrounding Joseph's pit/removal Definitely pre-Islamic.
Jubilees, Josephus and Late Antique Jewish/Christian interpretation demonstrate extensive rewriting of Genesis 37.
Level C — Water-drawer lowers bucket and discovers Joseph This is our actual Qur'an 12:19 feature.
Secure pre-Islamic witness presently: NOT VERIFIED.
8. This makes Q 12:19 more interesting, not less The Qur'an gives a remarkably specific scene:
Joseph was removed from the pit.
It's a miniature narrative scene with its own causal mechanism.
And at present we cannot securely push that complete mechanism into a surviving pre-Islamic Jewish or Christian text.
That distinction needs to survive in the database.
QB-0241 — CORRECTED PERMANENT RECORD Title Joseph's Discovery by the Caravan Water-Drawer
Joseph is placed in an empty pit/cistern explicitly containing no water.
Passing merchants subsequently become involved in his removal/sale.
no accidental discovery through water drawing.
Second Temple evidence Jubilees: no bucket-discovery mechanism.
Late Antique Jewish evidence Jewish interpretation substantially expands and harmonizes Joseph's pit/removal narrative.
No securely datable pre-Islamic Jewish witness for the complete bucket-discovery mechanism has yet been verified.
Later/complex Palestinian Targumic traditions cannot automatically be projected backward before Islam without independent chronological evidence.
Pre-Islamic Christian evidence Expanded Joseph traditions certainly circulated in Syriac/Greek Christianity.
No securely datable pre-Islamic Christian witness containing the complete water-drawer → bucket → Joseph-discovery mechanism has presently been verified.
EXPANDED JOSEPH PIT TRADITIONS BEFORE ISLAM: CERTAIN.
EXACT WATER-DRAWER/BUCKET DISCOVERY BEFORE ISLAM: NOT CURRENTLY DEMONSTRATED.
LATER JEWISH/TARGUMIC PARALLELS: relevant but chronologically insufficient by themselves.
DIRECT QUR'AN ↔ JEWISH/CHRISTIAN TEXTUAL DEPENDENCE: NOT DEMONSTRATED.
LOST ORAL PRE-ISLAMIC TRADITION: possible but unevidenced.
QB-0241 — bucket discovery: ⚠️ later/complex parallels exist, but exact pre-Islamic attestation not demonstrated
That correction should replace the stronger claim in my immediately preceding analysis so we don't carry an unsupported source-history conclusion into the frozen dataset.
Great. Next is Surah 12:20–22. We need to finish the sale question left open at 12:20, then follow Joseph into Egypt.
Surah 12:20 — Who actually sold Joseph? The verse says:
“And they sold him for a paltry price—a few counted dirhams—and they had little interest in him.”
The immediately preceding plural actors in 12:19 are the caravan people:
“A caravan came, and they sent their water-drawer…”
On the straightforward narrative reading, the grammatical continuity strongly favors:
caravan/travelers discover Joseph → conceal him as merchandise → sell him cheaply.
That means we can now resolve QB-0238 more firmly.

QB-0243 — Possible adoption of Joseph Genesis Joseph becomes:
Qur'an The purchaser immediately sees unusual potential:
“Perhaps he may benefit us, or we may take him as a son.”
But this phrase should immediately remind us of another biblical figure.
Moses In the Qur'an's Moses story, Pharaoh's wife says of the infant Moses:
“A comfort of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him. Perhaps he may benefit us, or we may take him as a son.”
It is essentially the same wording.
QI? No — this is deliberate literary intertext Joseph:
foreign/separated boy → Egypt → enters powerful household → “perhaps he may benefit us” → “or we may take him as a son.”
foreign/endangered infant → Egyptian royal household → “perhaps he may benefit us” → “or we may take him as a son.”
The Qur'an deliberately connects the two stories linguistically.
QB-0243                 Qur'anic purchaser considers adopting Joseph; Genesis          Qur'anic addition has no adoption proposal
QB-0243 — Joseph as a possible adopted son 1. Genesis gives us no adoption Genesis 39:1–6 presents the progression clearly:
→ Potiphar appoints him over his household
Nor does Genesis portray the purchase as motivated by childlessness or adoption.
So the Qur'anic adoption possibility does not come from canonical Genesis.
2. Jubilees — no adoption Jubilees greatly abbreviates this stage.
Joseph is sold into Egypt and enters Potiphar's household, but I find no tradition in which Potiphar purchases him because:
“perhaps he will benefit us, or we will take him as a son.”
Nor is Joseph made Potiphar's adopted son.
3. Josephus — important control, but still no adoption Josephus embellishes Joseph's story substantially.
Joseph becomes successful in Potiphar's household because of his abilities and character.
But again, the relationship remains essentially:
I find no securely attested Josephus passage in which Potiphar proposes adopting Joseph as his son.
This matters because Josephus is perfectly willing to expand biblical characterization; nevertheless, the Qur'anic adoption proposal isn't present there.
4. Testament of Joseph — no Potiphar adoption The Testament of Joseph is particularly relevant because it greatly expands Joseph's Egyptian experience, especially his sexual temptation and virtue.
But it does not give us the Qur'anic:
“Perhaps we may take him as a son.”
Its interests lie elsewhere—Joseph's chastity, suffering, resistance to temptation and divine faithfulness.
5. Genesis Rabbah — Joseph's rise is expanded, but not into adoption Rabbinic interpretation develops Joseph's extraordinary success in Potiphar's house.
That can certainly produce something resembling favored household status.
But that is not enough for our test.
I do not find a securely identifiable Genesis Rabbah passage giving the second.
PRE-ISLAMIC RABBINIC ADOPTION PARALLEL: NOT DEMONSTRATED.
6. Syriac Christian Joseph literature This was the most important place to check because Syriac Joseph traditions have already given us genuine extrabiblical parallels.
There are elaborate pre-Islamic Syriac treatments of:
But I do not find a securely datable pre-Islamic Syriac passage giving the precise idea:
Potiphar purchases Joseph and contemplates taking him as a son.
That's especially noteworthy because the Syriac tradition elaborates Joseph heavily.
So at our present evidentiary standard:
PRE-ISLAMIC CHRISTIAN ADOPTION PARALLEL: NOT DEMONSTRATED.
7. Now compare Qur'an 12:21 directly with Qur'an 28:9 This is where the evidence becomes much stronger.
Joseph — Q 12:21 The Egyptian purchaser says:
“Perhaps he may benefit us, or we may take him as a son.”
“Perhaps he may benefit us, or we may take him as a son.”
That makes accidental resemblance extremely unlikely.
QB-0243 — FINAL UPDATED RECORD Title The Egyptian Purchaser Considers Taking Joseph as a Son
Genesis Potiphar purchases Joseph as a slave.
Joseph becomes favored servant and administrator.
Second Temple Jewish evidence Jubilees: no adoption parallel located.
Testament of Joseph: no Potiphar adoption parallel located.
Rabbinic Jewish evidence Pre-Islamic/Late Antique Jewish interpretation greatly develops Joseph's Egyptian experience, but no securely datable Potiphar-adopts-Joseph tradition presently located.
Pre-Islamic Christian/Syriac evidence Extensive Joseph elaboration exists, but no securely datable adoption parallel presently located.
Q28:9 contains exactly the same clause concerning Moses.
Biblical Moses comparison Exodus 2:10 explicitly says Moses:
Classification PRE-ISLAMIC JOSEPH-ADOPTION PARALLEL: NOT CURRENTLY DEMONSTRATED.
EXACT QUR'ANIC JOSEPH–MOSES VERBAL LINK: CONFIRMED.
DELIBERATE QUR'ANIC JOSEPH–MOSES LITERARY LINKAGE: VERY STRONGLY SUPPORTED.
DIRECT SOURCE/COMPOSITIONAL MECHANISM: cannot be demonstrated.
This gives us a useful contrast with our last two investigations:
Untorn shirt — QB-0237: ✅ pre-Islamic extrabiblical parallel demonstrated.
Bucket discovery — QB-0241: ⚠ exact pre-Islamic parallel not demonstrated.

Joseph adoption — QB-0243/QB-0245: ⚠ no pre-Islamic Joseph adoption parallel demonstrated, but we have something arguably more informative: an explicit biblical Moses adoption tradition plus an exact Qur'anic Joseph–Moses verbal correspondence.

So for 12:21, the evidence currently points more strongly toward Qur'an-internal literary restructuring of the biblical traditions than toward preservation of a known pre-Islamic Joseph-adoption story.

We can now move into 12:23, where the Potiphar's-wife episode opens an exceptionally rich comparison: Genesis, the Testament of Joseph, Josephus, Philo, rabbinic literature, Syriac Christianity, and the Qur'an all preserve significantly different versions of Joseph's sexual temptation.
We now enter Surah 12:23–25, where the Qur'an's Joseph narrative begins diverging from Genesis in particularly interesting ways.
12:23 — The woman attempts to seduce Joseph The Qur'an says:
‫َو َراَو َدْت ُه اَّل ِتي ُه َو ِف ي َبْي ِتَه ا َع ن َّن ْفِس ِه َو َغ َّل َق ِت اْلَأْبَو اَب َو َق اَل ْت َه ْيَت َل َك‬

Your husband/my master has treated me well; I cannot betray him.
The second reading creates a striking parallel with Genesis.
Genesis Joseph tells the woman that her husband has entrusted virtually everything to him and withheld only her because she is his wife. He then asks:
how could he commit this great wrong and sin against God?                       Sefaria

Joseph invokes his rabb/master/Lord, good treatment, and concludes:

Then comes 12:24 — one of the most disputed Joseph verses in the Qur'an Arabic:
“She certainly desired/intended him, and he desired/intended her, had he not seen the proof/sign of his Lord.”

No explicit statement that Joseph desires/intends the woman.

Pre-Islamic/early Jewish interpretive trajectory Jewish interpreters developed traditions in which Joseph's resistance was more psychologically complicated and in some versions he approached the point of yielding before being stopped by a reminder/sign associated with his father.
Qur'an 12:24 Joseph's hamm is immediately followed by:
“had he not seen the burhān of his Lord.”
That combination is potentially extremely important.
Because later Jewish material famously has Joseph's father's image/vision appear at the critical moment and prevent the transgression.
If that tradition can be securely dated before Islam, we could have another parallel on the level of the untorn shirt.
But chronology must be tested before we say that.
The Qur'an itself explains God's intervention The verse continues:
“Thus [We acted] that We might turn away from him evil and sexual immorality/indecency.”
“Indeed, he was among Our chosen/sincere servants.”
It explicitly attributes his escape from sexual wrongdoing to divine intervention/protection.

QB-0250 — Joseph's garment during the attempted seduction Genesis Woman grabs garment.
Joseph leaves it behind entirely and escapes.
Garment becomes apparent evidence against Joseph.
Qur'an Woman grabs Joseph from behind.
The shirt tears at the back.
The direction of the tear will become evidence for Joseph's innocence.
This is one of the clearest transformations we've encountered.
Classification STRONG SHARED MOTIF + MAJOR QUR'ANIC REVERSAL OF EVIDENTIARY FUNCTION.
And this dramatically strengthens QDISC-1246, our garment motif.
Look at the transformation Genesis 37 Joseph's garment → false evidence → Jacob is deceived.
Genesis 39 Joseph's garment → false evidence → Joseph is accused.
Qur'an 12:18 Joseph's shirt + false blood → false evidence → Jacob rejects deception.
Qur'an 12:25–28 Joseph's torn shirt → woman attempts false accusation → physical evidence exposes deception.
The Qur'an repeatedly converts the garment from something that successfully enables deception in Genesis into something through which truth becomes recoverable.
That's now a very strong literary finding.
QB-0250                  Genesis garment left with woman and used against Joseph;          Major narrative/evidentiary Qur'an shirt torn from behind and becomes evidence for him        reversal
QB-0250 — UPGRADED Genesis Garment remains with woman.
She uses it as corroborating evidence.
Qur'an Shirt remains on Joseph but is torn from behind.
This is no longer merely a narrative variation.
It is an evidentiary inversion of Genesis 39.
Classification MAJOR QUR'ANIC RESTRUCTURING OF SHARED BIBLICAL MOTIF.
But now a major question appears If Joseph has been proven innocent:
Why does he eventually go to prison?
In Genesis, the answer is straightforward:
Potiphar apparently accepts his wife's accusation and has Joseph imprisoned.
But the Qur'an has just established:
Yet Joseph will still end up imprisoned in 12:35.
That means the Qur'an must supply a different reason for Joseph's imprisonment.
This is going to become a major Bible–Qur'an divergence.
